#!/bin/bash
# build.sh -- Compile and run a SNOBOL4 .plsw program via the
# devgroup-shared toolchain.
#
# Usage: ./scripts/build.sh [include/*.msw ...] src/program.plsw
#
# Tooling (all PATH-resolved):
#   pl-sw        -- PL/SW compiler (cor24-emu --lgo plsw.lgo wrapper)
#   cor24-asm    -- assembler: .s -> .lgo (and optionally .bin/.lst)
#   cor24-emu    -- runtime: cor24-emu --lgo <prog>.lgo
#
# Outputs build/<name>.s (assembly) and build/<name>.lgo (loadable).

set -euo pipefail

if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 [include/*.msw ...] src/program.plsw" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Separate .msw macros, .plsw library includes, and the .plsw main.
# Convention: every .msw is a macro (registered under its full
# basename so %INCLUDE NAME works the way descr.msw / heap.msw etc.
# already do). Every .plsw EXCEPT the last is a library include
# (registered under its bare stem so %INCLUDE SNOLIB matches
# src/snolib.plsw). The last .plsw on the command line is MAIN.
MACROS=()
LIB_PLSW=()
MAIN=""
PLSW_ARGS=()
for f in "$@"; do
    case "$f" in
        *.msw)  MACROS+=("$f") ;;
        *.plsw) PLSW_ARGS+=("$f") ;;
        *) echo "Error: unknown file type: $f" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
done

if [ ${#PLSW_ARGS[@]} -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Error: no .plsw file specified" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Last .plsw is MAIN; earlier .plsw files become library includes.
MAIN="${PLSW_ARGS[$((${#PLSW_ARGS[@]} - 1))]}"
for ((i = 0; i < ${#PLSW_ARGS[@]} - 1; i++)); do
    LIB_PLSW+=("${PLSW_ARGS[$i]}")
done

BASENAME=$(basename "$MAIN" .plsw)
mkdir -p build

# Build UART input for the compiler (FILE:/SOURCE: protocol).
# .msw macros are registered under basename (e.g. "descr.msw");
# .plsw library includes are registered under their bare stem
# (e.g. "snolib") so the source can do `%INCLUDE snolib;`.
build_input() {
    printf 'c\n'
    if [ ${#MACROS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        for m in "${MACROS[@]}"; do
            printf 'FILE:%s\n' "$(basename "$m")"
            cat "$m"
            printf '\x1E'
        done
    fi
    if [ ${#LIB_PLSW[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        for l in "${LIB_PLSW[@]}"; do
            printf 'FILE:%s\n' "$(basename "$l" .plsw)"
            cat "$l"
            printf '\x1E'
        done
    fi
    if [ ${#MACROS[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ ${#LIB_PLSW[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        printf 'SOURCE:\n'
    fi
    cat "$MAIN"
    printf '\x04'
}

INPUT=$(build_input)

# Compile via pl-sw (wraps cor24-emu --lgo plsw.lgo)
echo "=== Compiling $BASENAME ===" >&2
echo "  Macros: ${MACROS[*]:-none}" >&2
echo "  Source: $MAIN" >&2

COMPILER_OUT=$(pl-sw -u "$INPUT" -n 1000000000 -t 600 --speed 0 2>&1)
UART_OUT=$(echo "$COMPILER_OUT" | sed -n '/^UART output:/,/^Executed /{/^Executed /d;p;}' | sed '1s/^UART output: //')

# Check for errors
if echo "$UART_OUT" | grep -q "compilation failed\|COMPILE ERROR\|ERROR:"; then
    echo "Compilation FAILED:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" | grep -E "ERROR:|failed|error" >&2
    echo "" >&2
    echo "Full compiler output:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Show registered includes
echo "$UART_OUT" | grep "registered:" >&2 || true

# Extract assembly
START_MARKER="--- generated assembly ---"
END_MARKER="--- end assembly ---"
ASM=$(echo "$UART_OUT" | sed -n "/$START_MARKER/,/$END_MARKER/{/$START_MARKER/d;/$END_MARKER/d;p;}")

if [ -z "$ASM" ]; then
    echo "Error: no assembly output found" >&2
    echo "Full compiler output:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Save assembly
OUT_S="build/${BASENAME}.s"
echo "$ASM" > "$OUT_S"
ASM_LINES=$(echo "$ASM" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
echo "  Assembly: $ASM_LINES lines -> $OUT_S" >&2

# Assemble to .lgo. Tolerate failure: build-modular.sh calls this script
# only to obtain $OUT_S for individual modules, where standalone assembly
# of a library module may have unresolved cross-module labels.
OUT_LGO="build/${BASENAME}.lgo"
ASM_OUT=$(cor24-asm "$OUT_S" -o "$OUT_LGO" 2>&1) || {
    echo "=== Assembly skipped/failed for $BASENAME ===" >&2
    echo "$ASM_OUT" >&2
    exit 0
}

echo "=== Running $BASENAME ===" >&2
RUN_OUT=$(cor24-emu --lgo "$OUT_LGO" -n 100000000 -t 60 --speed 0 --dump 2>&1)

# Save dump
OUT_DUMP="build/${BASENAME}-dump.txt"
echo "$RUN_OUT" > "$OUT_DUMP"

# Show program UART output
PROG_OUT=$(echo "$RUN_OUT" | sed -n '/^UART output:/,/^Executed /{/^Executed /d;p;}' | sed '1s/^UART output: //')
if [ -n "$PROG_OUT" ]; then
    echo "$PROG_OUT"
fi

# Show execution stats
echo "$RUN_OUT" | grep -E "^  Instructions:|^  Halted:" >&2 || true

if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 [include/*.msw ...] src/program.plsw" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Separate .msw and .plsw files
MACROS=()
MAIN=""
for f in "$@"; do
    case "$f" in
        *.msw) MACROS+=("$f") ;;
        *.plsw) MAIN="$f" ;;
        *) echo "Error: unknown file type: $f" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
done

if [ -z "$MAIN" ]; then
    echo "Error: no .plsw file specified" >&2
    exit 1
fi

BASENAME=$(basename "$MAIN" .plsw)
mkdir -p build

# Build UART input for the compiler (FILE:/SOURCE: protocol)
build_input() {
    printf 'c\n'
    if [ ${#MACROS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        for m in "${MACROS[@]}"; do
            printf 'FILE:%s\n' "$(basename "$m")"
            cat "$m"
            printf '\x1E'
        done
        printf 'SOURCE:\n'
    fi
    cat "$MAIN"
    printf '\x04'
}

INPUT=$(build_input)

# Compile via pl-sw (wraps cor24-emu --lgo plsw.lgo)
echo "=== Compiling $BASENAME ===" >&2
echo "  Macros: ${MACROS[*]:-none}" >&2
echo "  Source: $MAIN" >&2

COMPILER_OUT=$(pl-sw -u "$INPUT" -n 1000000000 -t 600 --speed 0 2>&1)
UART_OUT=$(echo "$COMPILER_OUT" | sed -n '/^UART output:/,/^Executed /{/^Executed /d;p;}' | sed '1s/^UART output: //')

# Check for errors
if echo "$UART_OUT" | grep -q "compilation failed\|COMPILE ERROR\|ERROR:"; then
    echo "Compilation FAILED:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" | grep -E "ERROR:|failed|error" >&2
    echo "" >&2
    echo "Full compiler output:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Show registered includes
echo "$UART_OUT" | grep "registered:" >&2 || true

# Extract assembly
START_MARKER="--- generated assembly ---"
END_MARKER="--- end assembly ---"
ASM=$(echo "$UART_OUT" | sed -n "/$START_MARKER/,/$END_MARKER/{/$START_MARKER/d;/$END_MARKER/d;p;}")

if [ -z "$ASM" ]; then
    echo "Error: no assembly output found" >&2
    echo "Full compiler output:" >&2
    echo "$UART_OUT" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Save assembly
OUT_S="build/${BASENAME}.s"
echo "$ASM" > "$OUT_S"
ASM_LINES=$(echo "$ASM" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
echo "  Assembly: $ASM_LINES lines -> $OUT_S" >&2

# Assemble to .lgo. Tolerate failure: build-modular.sh calls this script
# only to obtain $OUT_S for individual modules, where standalone assembly
# of a library module may have unresolved cross-module labels.
OUT_LGO="build/${BASENAME}.lgo"
ASM_OUT=$(cor24-asm "$OUT_S" -o "$OUT_LGO" 2>&1) || {
    echo "=== Assembly skipped/failed for $BASENAME ===" >&2
    echo "$ASM_OUT" >&2
    exit 0
}

echo "=== Running $BASENAME ===" >&2
RUN_OUT=$(cor24-emu --lgo "$OUT_LGO" -n 100000000 -t 60 --speed 0 --dump 2>&1)

# Save dump
OUT_DUMP="build/${BASENAME}-dump.txt"
echo "$RUN_OUT" > "$OUT_DUMP"

# Show program UART output
PROG_OUT=$(echo "$RUN_OUT" | sed -n '/^UART output:/,/^Executed /{/^Executed /d;p;}' | sed '1s/^UART output: //')
if [ -n "$PROG_OUT" ]; then
    echo "$PROG_OUT"
fi

# Show execution stats
echo "$RUN_OUT" | grep -E "^  Instructions:|^  Halted:" >&2 || true

# SNOBOL4 on PL/SW for COR24

# Build the SNOBOL4 interpreter (modular: sno_main + sno_util + sno_lex + sno_exec)
build:
    bash scripts/build-modular.sh

# Force a full rebuild of the interpreter, ignoring the dep manifest
rebuild:
    bash scripts/build-modular.sh -f

# Produce the canonical shippable .lgo artifact for the shared toolchain.
# The modular linker (link24) emits a raw .bin; bin-to-lgo.sh wraps it as
# the L-record text format mike installs to work/lib/cor24/snobol4.lgo.
#
# NOTE: cor24-emu currently ignores --load-binary when --lgo is set
# (https://... -- dcemu brief pending). Until that's fixed, the runtime
# wrapper should use:  cor24-emu --load-binary snobol4.bin@0 --entry 0
# rather than the planned `cor24-emu --lgo snobol4.lgo`. The .lgo is
# shippable; only the auxiliary-data load path needs the dcemu fix.
build-lgo: build
    bash scripts/bin-to-lgo.sh build/snobol4.bin build/snobol4.lgo
    @echo "Built build/snobol4.lgo ($(wc -c < build/snobol4.lgo) bytes, $(wc -l < build/snobol4.lgo) records)"

# tools/briefs/

Saga briefs for the COR24 multi-agent ecosystem. Each brief is a self-contained spec for a saga: the agent reads it, develops on `feat/<slug>`, renames to `pr/<slug>` when ready, signals mike, mike relays.

## How briefs work

- **Filename convention:** `<target>-<saga-slug>.md`. `<target>` is either a single agent (e.g. `dcxas-cor24-asm-cli.md`) or a generic prefix (`dc-`, `dw-`) for multi-agent briefs.
- **Branch convention — feat→pr rename:**
  - **`feat/<slug>`** = work-in-progress. Agents create this with `dg-new-feature <slug>` (which cuts from `origin/dev`).
  - **`pr/<slug>`** = signal that the saga is **ready for relay**. Created by renaming `feat/<slug>` → `pr/<slug>` via `dg-mark-pr` once the work is complete and tested.
  - The branch shape **is** the readiness signal. Never start a saga on `pr/<slug>` directly — `dg-list-pr` would see it as ready and `dg-relay` could integrate WIP.
- **Workflow:** agent reads brief → `dg-new-feature <slug>` (creates `feat/<slug>` from `dev`) → implements + tests → `dg-mark-pr` (renames to `pr/<slug>`) → signals mike → mike `dg-relay`s → mike promotes `dev → main` when ready (separate, on-demand step).
- **Agents may draft cross-repo briefs.** If an agent diagnoses a blocker in another repo (e.g. a tc24r limitation), they can draft a brief for the responsible agent and drop it directly here. Mike reviews at relay time. See `feedback_agent_drafted_briefs.md` in the project memory.
- **Permissions:** dir is `drwxrwsr-x mike:devgroup`. Mike-authored briefs have mode `640 mike:devgroup`. Agent-drafted briefs inherit `<agent>:devgroup` ownership.

## 🏛️ Architecture: compilers, wrappers, demos

Each language repo (`sw-cor24-<lang>`) builds **a compiler/interpreter** for that language on COR24. That compiler is the repo's main artifact. Demos under `examples/` exercise the compiler.

Wrappers on PATH (`work/bin/<lang>`) invoke the compiler. **Two valid packagings for the shipped compiler** — mike picks at install time:

- **Bundled `.lgo`** (e.g. `plsw.lgo`): single self-contained image. Wrapper is a thin pass-through: `exec cor24-emu --lgo $TOOLROOT/../lib/cor24/<lang>.lgo "$@"`.
- **Script-composed**: wrapper is a shell script that runs `cor24-emu --lgo <interpreter>.lgo --load-binary <compiler>.sno@<addr> ...`. Useful when the compiler is itself a program in another language that runs inside an interpreter image (e.g. Fortran-in-SNOBOL4 — `fortran` could compose `snobol4.lgo` + `fortran-compiler.sno` at runtime instead of pre-bundling).

Both packagings are equivalent for users; the choice is about build-time bundling. Future briefs/sagas don't constrain agents to one or the other.

Demos and demo outputs (e.g. `examples/hello.f`, `examples/hello.lgo`) live in the repo's own `examples/` directory and are **not** installed to `work/lib/cor24/` — only compilers/interpreters live there.

## 🚀 Current critical path — Fortran hello-world live demo

Four briefs unblock the Fortran demo at `https://sw-embed.github.io/web-sw-cor24-fortran/`:

1. **`dcemu-lgo-load-binary-merge.md`** — fixes a 1-line bug where `cor24-emu --lgo X.lgo --load-binary Y@addr` silently drops the `--load-binary`. Discovered by dcsno; agent-drafted brief; precise root-cause + repro. **Critical for the canonical SNOBOL4 wrapper to work.** dcemu plans to tackle this after finishing prior saga work.
2. **`dcsno-bootstrap-snobol4-toolchain.md`** — produces `snobol4.lgo`. Can ship NOW with a documented workaround using the `--load-binary snobol4.bin@0` path; flip to the canonical `--lgo` wrapper after dcemu's fix lands (small follow-up saga).
3. **`dcftn-fortran-hello-world.md`** — produces `examples/hello.lgo` (Path A: hand-write OK; full FTI-0 compiler is a parallel effort).
4. **`dwftn-hello-world-demo.md`** — Yew/WASM web frontend embedding the .lgo.

content:
there may be a bug with conditional branching.
Note:
I have a snobol4 implementation but an ai coding agent complained:
Found it — combined :S(...) :F(...) doesn't work in this dialect. Both branches always fire :S. Now I see SUBSTR/IDENT/RAWINPUT all
  work correctly with single-direction gotos. My normalize.sno doesn't use combined gotos, so the bug must be elsewhere. Building it up
  incrementally.

I’ll treat this as a debugging/design review of the agent’s conclusion: what the statement likely means, what is plausible in SNOBOL4 semantics, and how to isolate whether the dialect, the test, or the agent is wrong.

Thought for 6s

The agent’s claim is suspiciously worded.

In standard SNOBOL4, combined conditional transfer is valid:

        X "YES"        :S(SUCCESS)F(FAIL)

Only one branch should be taken, because the statement either succeeds or fails. References describe :S(label1)F(label2) as the normal “goto depending on success/failure” form.

So if your implementation/dialect makes both branches “fire” as :S, likely causes are:

Likely bug classes
Parser bug
It tokenizes :S(A)F(B) as two independent transfers.
Or it loses the F qualifier and treats both as success transfers.

Codegen/VM bug

The AST is correct, but emitted branch opcodes both test success.
Example bad lowering:
if success goto A
if success goto B   ; should be if failure goto B
Statement-status lifetime bug
The first transfer evaluation mutates/overwrites the success/failure flag before the second transfer is considered.
Agent test bug
They may have tested with fall-through labels arranged so it appears both fired.
In SNOBOL-style flow, a success branch that lands immediately before the failure label can look like both ran.
Minimal regression test

Use labels that cannot fall through into each other:

        "ABC" "A"       :S(S_OK)F(S_BAD)

S_OK    OUTPUT = "success branch"
        :(END)

S_BAD   OUTPUT = "failure branch"
        :(END)

END

Expected:

success branch

And failure case:

        "ABC" "Z"       :S(F_BAD)F(F_OK)

F_OK    OUTPUT = "failure branch"
        :(END)

F_BAD   OUTPUT = "success branch"
        :(END)

END

Expected:

failure branch
What I’d tell the agent

Standard SNOBOL4 supports combined :S(...)F(...); if this dialect does not, document it as a dialect limitation. But first verify with a no-fallthrough test. If both branches behave as success branches, inspect transfer parsing and branch-code generation for F(...) after an S(...).

The important point: your normalize.sno avoiding combined gotos does not prove the bug is elsewhere unless every callee/helper/library file also avoids them, and unless the agent’s “both branches always fire :S” conclusion was based on a no-fallthrough test.
and look for a bri⟧at tools/briefs/dcsno-combined-goto-parser.md and verify that your implementation is not valid (or explain why it is in fact valid as is).  Plan to fix it if needed.

1	# Brief: SNOBOL4 parser drops second goto in combined `:S(...):F(...)` form
2	
3	**Owner:** dcsno
4	**Branch:** `pr/combined-goto-parser`
5	**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
6	**Discovered by:** dcftn during `milestone-1-fortran-compiler` saga (2026-05-08).
7	**Affects:** any SNOBOL4 program that uses combined success/failure
8	transfer on a single statement, e.g.
9	
10	```
11	        SUBJECT pattern    :S(MATCH):F(NOMATCH)
12	        IDENT(X, Y)        :S(SAME):F(DIFF)
13	```
14	
15	This is part of the documented dialect surface
16	(`examples/pattern-tutorial.sno` documents the form
17	`SUBJECT  pattern... :S(label) :F(label)`) and is part of standard
18	SNOBOL4 (Bell Labs Macro Implementation, SPITBOL, Catspaw).
19	Programs that rely on it must be rewritten to use single-direction
20	gotos until the fix lands -- bug-prone and clutters the source.
21	
22	## Symptom
23	
24	When a statement specifies both `:S(...)` and `:F(...)` (with or
25	without a separating space, with or without a colon prefix on the
26	second goto), the parser attaches **only the first goto** and
27	silently drops the second.
28	
29	The bug is parser-only -- predicate evaluation, the success/failure
30	flag, and goto dispatch all work correctly when given a properly-
31	attached goto. With single-direction gotos (`:S(LBL)` alone,
32	`:F(LBL)` alone), control flow is correct.
33	
34	The bug is silent: no warning, no error, just lost branches.
35	Programs appear to "work" until they exercise the dropped goto, at
36	which point they fall through to the next statement (often into a
37	wrong-label block) and produce nonsense.
38	
39	## Repro (no-fallthrough regression -- isolates parser from flow artifacts)
40	
41	Earlier diagnosis attempts used label sequences that allowed silent
42	fallthrough into the success-branch's body, which masked parser-
43	bug behavior as "always-S-fires." The disambiguating form below
44	puts an explicit `:(EX)` between the predicate and the labelled
45	branches so neither label can be entered by fallthrough:
46	
47	```
48	$ cat /tmp/goto.sno
49	        IDENT('A', 'B')                         :S(SOK):F(SBAD)
50	        OUTPUT = 'fallthrough -- no goto fired'  :(EX)
51	SOK     OUTPUT = 'S branch fired'                :(EX)
52	SBAD    OUTPUT = 'F branch fired'                :(EX)
53	EX      END
54	
55	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/goto.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
56	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
57	fallthrough -- no goto fired
58	```
59	
60	Standard SNOBOL4 says: `IDENT('A','B')` fails, `:F(SBAD)` fires,
61	output `F branch fired`. Observed: fallthrough -- neither goto
62	fired, so `:F(SBAD)` was never attached to the statement.
63	
64	Inverse with a succeeding predicate works correctly:
65	
66	```
67	$ cat /tmp/goto2.sno
68	        IDENT('A', 'A')                         :S(SOK):F(SBAD)
69	        OUTPUT = 'fallthrough -- no goto fired'  :(EX)
70	SOK     OUTPUT = 'S branch fired'                :(EX)
71	SBAD    OUTPUT = 'F branch fired'                :(EX)
72	EX      END
73	
74	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/goto2.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
75	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
76	S branch fired
77	```
78	
79	This proves `:S(SOK)` IS attached and works. Only the trailing
80	`:F(SBAD)` is dropped on the failing-predicate path.
81	
82	## Root cause hint (per source read on 2026-05-08)
83	
84	`src/sno_lex.plsw`:
85	
86	- `S_GTYP(S)` is a single-valued field initialised at line 372:
87	  `S_GTYP(S) = GT_NONE;`. Type values seen in source:
88	  `GT_NONE`, `GT_SUCC`, `GT_FAIL`, `GT_UNCOND`, `GT_RET`, `GT_FRET`.
89	  There is no enum value for "both S and F." The per-statement
90	  representation carries one goto, not two.
91	- Two TK_COLON handlers (`sno_lex.plsw:1069..` and `:1113..`).
92	  Each sets `S_GTYP(S) = GT_SUCC | GT_FAIL | GT_UNCOND | ...` once.
93	  Neither loops over multiple `:S/:F/:` colons after the first.
94	  Whichever colon is parsed first wins; subsequent colons (even
95	  followed by a valid goto) are silently consumed but not stored.
96	
97	So the bug is structural: the parsed-statement representation
98	cannot carry both an S-branch and an F-branch.
99	
100	## Fix shape
101	
102	Two-line summary:
103	
104	1. Extend the per-statement state to carry both an S-target and
105	   an F-target (separate label slots, or a small per-goto table).
106	2. Update the TK_COLON handler to loop and consume `:S(...) :F(...)`
107	   variants (with/without space, with/without second-colon).
108	
109	Concrete: rather than a single `S_GTYP / S_GLBL` pair, hold up to
110	two structured goto records:
111	
112	- `S_GLBL_S(S)` -- label index, or `-1` for "none".
113	- `S_GLBL_F(S)` -- label index, or `-1` for "none".
114	- Optionally keep `S_GTYP(S)` for `GT_UNCOND / GT_RET / GT_FRET`
115	  (which are mutually exclusive with S/F).
116	
117	The dispatcher (`src/sno_exec.plsw`) currently jumps based on
118	`S_GTYP(S)`. Update it to:
119	
120	- If predicate succeeded and `S_GLBL_S(S) >= 0`, jump there.
121	- If predicate failed and `S_GLBL_F(S) >= 0`, jump there.
122	- Otherwise fall through.
123	
124	(Plus existing UNCOND / RET / FRET handling, unchanged.)
125	
126	## Accepted goto-syntax variants (per standard SNOBOL4)
127	
128	All four of these forms must parse equivalently and produce the
129	same wired-up `S_GLBL_S` and `S_GLBL_F`:
130	
131	```
132	        STMT    :S(L1):F(L2)
133	        STMT    :S(L1) :F(L2)
134	        STMT    :S(L1)F(L2)        ; second goto without a colon prefix
135	        STMT    :F(L2):S(L1)        ; reversed order
136	```
137	
138	Single-direction forms (`:S(L1)` alone, `:F(L2)` alone, `:(L1)`,
139	`:RETURN`, `:FRETURN`) keep their current correct behaviour.
140	
141	## Tests to add
142	
143	Add to `examples/` or a dedicated test fixture set:
144	
145	1. **Combined goto, predicate FAILS, both branches present** --
146	   expect F to fire (the no-fallthrough form above).
147	2. **Combined goto, predicate SUCCEEDS, both branches present** --
148	   expect S to fire.
149	3. **No-colon-on-second-goto variant** -- `:S(L1) F(L2)` should
150	   behave identically to `:S(L1):F(L2)`.
151	4. **Reverse order** -- `:F(L1):S(L2)` should also work.
152	5. **Pattern-match form** -- `STR pattern :S(L1):F(L2)` (the form
153	   documented in `examples/pattern-tutorial.sno`).
154	6. **Pathological** -- `:S(L1):S(L2)` (two S targets) should
155	   either reject or document precedence; do not silently drop one.
156	
157	## What does NOT go in this PR
158	
159	- No new SNOBOL4 surface features.
160	- No changes to the success/failure flag mechanics -- those work.
161	- No changes to single-direction goto handling -- that works.
162	
163	## When done
164	
165	Push `pr/combined-goto-parser`. After mike relays + reinstalls
166	the snobol4 binary:
167	
168	- dcftn's `feat/m1-resume` saga can use combined gotos (more
169	  readable in normalize / classify / expr / lower / emit_plsw)
170	  instead of refactoring around single-direction-only gotos.
171	- Any other future SNOBOL4 program relying on the documented
172	  combined-goto form works as written.
173	
174	## Credit
175	
176	Bug class identified by an external reviewer who pushed back on a
177	sloppy first diagnosis from dcftn (which had assumed "always-S-
178	fires" based on a fallthrough artifact). The reviewer suggested
179	the no-fallthrough regression form which cleanly disambiguates
180	parser-bug from flag-bug from fallthrough; that form is what's
181	used above. Captured here so the next agent walking the same path
182	goes straight to the right diagnosis.
183

# Brief: SNOBOL4 parser drops second goto in combined `:S(...):F(...)` form

**Owner:** dcsno
**Branch:** `pr/combined-goto-parser`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
**Discovered by:** dcftn during `milestone-1-fortran-compiler` saga (2026-05-08).
**Affects:** any SNOBOL4 program that uses combined success/failure
transfer on a single statement, e.g.

```
        SUBJECT pattern    :S(MATCH):F(NOMATCH)
        IDENT(X, Y)        :S(SAME):F(DIFF)
```

This is part of the documented dialect surface
(`examples/pattern-tutorial.sno` documents the form
`SUBJECT  pattern... :S(label) :F(label)`) and is part of standard
SNOBOL4 (Bell Labs Macro Implementation, SPITBOL, Catspaw).
Programs that rely on it must be rewritten to use single-direction
gotos until the fix lands -- bug-prone and clutters the source.

## Symptom

When a statement specifies both `:S(...)` and `:F(...)` (with or
without a separating space, with or without a colon prefix on the
second goto), the parser attaches **only the first goto** and
silently drops the second.

The bug is parser-only -- predicate evaluation, the success/failure
flag, and goto dispatch all work correctly when given a properly-
attached goto. With single-direction gotos (`:S(LBL)` alone,
`:F(LBL)` alone), control flow is correct.

The bug is silent: no warning, no error, just lost branches.
Programs appear to "work" until they exercise the dropped goto, at
which point they fall through to the next statement (often into a
wrong-label block) and produce nonsense.

## Repro (no-fallthrough regression -- isolates parser from flow artifacts)

Earlier diagnosis attempts used label sequences that allowed silent
fallthrough into the success-branch's body, which masked parser-
bug behavior as "always-S-fires." The disambiguating form below
puts an explicit `:(EX)` between the predicate and the labelled
branches so neither label can be entered by fallthrough:

```
$ cat /tmp/goto.sno
        IDENT('A', 'B')                         :S(SOK):F(SBAD)
        OUTPUT = 'fallthrough -- no goto fired'  :(EX)
SOK     OUTPUT = 'S branch fired'                :(EX)
SBAD    OUTPUT = 'F branch fired'                :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/goto.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
fallthrough -- no goto fired
```

Standard SNOBOL4 says: `IDENT('A','B')` fails, `:F(SBAD)` fires,
output `F branch fired`. Observed: fallthrough -- neither goto
fired, so `:F(SBAD)` was never attached to the statement.

Inverse with a succeeding predicate works correctly:

```
$ cat /tmp/goto2.sno
        IDENT('A', 'A')                         :S(SOK):F(SBAD)
        OUTPUT = 'fallthrough -- no goto fired'  :(EX)
SOK     OUTPUT = 'S branch fired'                :(EX)
SBAD    OUTPUT = 'F branch fired'                :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/goto2.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
S branch fired
```

This proves `:S(SOK)` IS attached and works. Only the trailing
`:F(SBAD)` is dropped on the failing-predicate path.

## Root cause hint (per source read on 2026-05-08)

`src/sno_lex.plsw`:

- `S_GTYP(S)` is a single-valued field initialised at line 372:
  `S_GTYP(S) = GT_NONE;`. Type values seen in source:
  `GT_NONE`, `GT_SUCC`, `GT_FAIL`, `GT_UNCOND`, `GT_RET`, `GT_FRET`.
  There is no enum value for "both S and F." The per-statement
  representation carries one goto, not two.
- Two TK_COLON handlers (`sno_lex.plsw:1069..` and `:1113..`).
  Each sets `S_GTYP(S) = GT_SUCC | GT_FAIL | GT_UNCOND | ...` once.
  Neither loops over multiple `:S/:F/:` colons after the first.
  Whichever colon is parsed first wins; subsequent colons (even
  followed by a valid goto) are silently consumed but not stored.

So the bug is structural: the parsed-statement representation
cannot carry both an S-branch and an F-branch.

## Fix shape

Two-line summary:

1. Extend the per-statement state to carry both an S-target and
   an F-target (separate label slots, or a small per-goto table).
2. Update the TK_COLON handler to loop and consume `:S(...) :F(...)`
   variants (with/without space, with/without second-colon).

Concrete: rather than a single `S_GTYP / S_GLBL` pair, hold up to
two structured goto records:

- `S_GLBL_S(S)` -- label index, or `-1` for "none".
- `S_GLBL_F(S)` -- label index, or `-1` for "none".
- Optionally keep `S_GTYP(S)` for `GT_UNCOND / GT_RET / GT_FRET`
  (which are mutually exclusive with S/F).

The dispatcher (`src/sno_exec.plsw`) currently jumps based on
`S_GTYP(S)`. Update it to:

- If predicate succeeded and `S_GLBL_S(S) >= 0`, jump there.
- If predicate failed and `S_GLBL_F(S) >= 0`, jump there.
- Otherwise fall through.

(Plus existing UNCOND / RET / FRET handling, unchanged.)

## Accepted goto-syntax variants (per standard SNOBOL4)

All four of these forms must parse equivalently and produce the
same wired-up `S_GLBL_S` and `S_GLBL_F`:

```
        STMT    :S(L1):F(L2)
        STMT    :S(L1) :F(L2)
        STMT    :S(L1)F(L2)        ; second goto without a colon prefix
        STMT    :F(L2):S(L1)        ; reversed order
```

Single-direction forms (`:S(L1)` alone, `:F(L2)` alone, `:(L1)`,
`:RETURN`, `:FRETURN`) keep their current correct behaviour.

## Tests to add

Add to `examples/` or a dedicated test fixture set:

1. **Combined goto, predicate FAILS, both branches present** --
   expect F to fire (the no-fallthrough form above).
2. **Combined goto, predicate SUCCEEDS, both branches present** --
   expect S to fire.
3. **No-colon-on-second-goto variant** -- `:S(L1) F(L2)` should
   behave identically to `:S(L1):F(L2)`.
4. **Reverse order** -- `:F(L1):S(L2)` should also work.
5. **Pattern-match form** -- `STR pattern :S(L1):F(L2)` (the form
   documented in `examples/pattern-tutorial.sno`).
6. **Pathological** -- `:S(L1):S(L2)` (two S targets) should
   either reject or document precedence; do not silently drop one.

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No new SNOBOL4 surface features.
- No changes to the success/failure flag mechanics -- those work.
- No changes to single-direction goto handling -- that works.

## When done

Push `pr/combined-goto-parser`. After mike relays + reinstalls
the snobol4 binary:

- dcftn's `feat/m1-resume` saga can use combined gotos (more
  readable in normalize / classify / expr / lower / emit_plsw)
  instead of refactoring around single-direction-only gotos.
- Any other future SNOBOL4 program relying on the documented
  combined-goto form works as written.

## Credit

Bug class identified by an external reviewer who pushed back on a
sloppy first diagnosis from dcftn (which had assumed "always-S-
fires" based on a fallthrough artifact). The reviewer suggested
the no-fallthrough regression form which cleanly disambiguates
parser-bug from flag-bug from fallthrough; that form is what's
used above. Captured here so the next agent walking the same path
goes straight to the right diagnosis.

content.description: Replace inline helper definitions in the two snolib test suites with %INCLUDE snolib (or build-time linking). Tests must still pass.

content.description: Run full test suite (both snolib tests must pass) and verify just build still produces a working interpreter (snolib not yet wired in -- that's step 2/3/4).

content.description: Onboarding flagged origin/dev does not exist yet. Bootstrap local dev (git switch -c dev origin/main), then cut pr/bootstrap-toolchain from dev. Use pr/ shape directly per coordinator's relay expectations.

content.description: Confirm pl-sw, cor24-asm, cor24-emu, link24, meta-gen, tc24r are PATH-resolved and that work/lib/cor24/plsw.lgo exists.

content.subject: Update scripts/build.sh per migration map
content.description: Replace cor24-run --assemble (and any $HOME/... paths) with the new PATH-resolved commands listed in the brief.

content.subject: Update scripts/build-modular.sh per migration map
content.description: Replace LINKER_DIR=$HOME/... LINK24/META_GEN paths and any cor24-run --assemble calls with PATH-resolved commands. Goal: produce build/snobol4.lgo via canonical pipeline (pl-sw -> cor24-asm).

content.subject: Run end-to-end build, verify build/snobol4.lgo
content.description: Run just rebuild and confirm canonical pipeline produces build/snobol4.lgo. Run smoke demos.

content.subject: Commit, signal ready on pr/bootstrap-toolchain
content.description: Commit changes on pr/bootstrap-toolchain branch and signal to coordinator (mike) that the branch is ready for relay. Do NOT push -- coordinator-only.

content.subject: Verify combined :S/:F goto bug with repro
content.description: Run the brief's no-fallthrough repro on current dev's snobol4.bin to confirm the parser drops the second goto. Both repros (failing and succeeding predicate) included.

content.subject: Plan parser/executor changes for combined gotos
content.description: Read sno_lex.plsw TK_COLON handlers (lines 1069, 1113), S_GTYP/S_GLBL state, sno_exec.plsw goto dispatch, snoglob.msw declarations. Design separate S_GLBL_S / S_GLBL_F slots with -1 sentinel, plus loop in TK_COLON handler. Document accepted goto-syntax variants.

content.subject: Implement combined goto parser+executor fix
content.description: Add S_GLBL_S/S_GLBL_F to snoglob.msw. Update lexer TK_COLON handler to loop and consume :S/:F (with/without colon prefix). Update executor dispatcher to use S_GLBL_S on success / S_GLBL_F on failure / fall through if both -1. Keep unconditional/return forms unchanged.

content.subject: Add branch-behavior demos and regression fixtures
content.description: Add examples/branch_*.sno demos covering: combined :S/:F with failing predicate (F fires), combined with succeeding predicate (S fires), no-colon-on-second variant, reverse order, pattern-match form, single-direction (regression). Wire into justfile.

content.subject: Validate full demo suite + commit + signal ready
content.description: Run just demos and just test. Confirm no regression in single-direction goto programs. Commit, rename feat/combined-goto-parser to pr/combined-goto-parser, signal mike.

git add include/snoglob.msw justfile src/sno_exec.plsw src/sno_lex.plsw examples/branches.sno && git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix: combined :S(...) :F(...) goto parser+executor

The lexer's two TK_COLON handlers each consumed one goto modifier
and silently dropped any subsequent ones, so a statement like
`IDENT(x,y) :S(L1):F(L2)` only attached :S(L1) -- :F(L2) was lost.
Programs that relied on the standard combined form (the SPITBOL /
Catspaw / Bell-Labs Macro Implementation surface, also documented
in our own examples/pattern-tutorial.sno) fell through to the
following statement on the dropped branch and produced nonsense.

Fix:

* snoglob.msw -- add S_GLBL_F + S_GOTO_OFF_F (just two new arrays;
  the per-statement INT-array footprint runs against the PL/SW
  EMIT_BUF_SIZE = 256KB ceiling, so we reuse the existing S_GLBL /
  S_GOTO_OFF for the primary branch instead of adding four).
* sno_lex.plsw -- factor goto parsing into a single PARSE_GOTOS
  helper called from both TK_COLON sites. Loops to consume every
  modifier, accepts `:S(L1):F(L2)`, `:S(L1) :F(L2)`, `:S(L1)F(L2)`
  (no second colon), `:F(L1):S(L2)` (reversed order), plus all the
  pre-existing single-direction / `:(L)` / `:(RETURN)` / `:(FRETURN)`
  forms unchanged. Reversed order is handled by rotating S_GLBL into
  S_GLBL_F when an :S target lands on top of an existing :F target.
* sno_exec.plsw -- when S_GTYP=GT_SUCC and S_GLBL_F>=0, emit
  OP_BR_SUCC followed by OP_BR_FAIL so the executor's success/fail
  flag dispatches naturally. FIXUP_GOTOS patches both the primary
  slot (via S_GOTO_OFF/S_GLBL) and the failure slot (via
  S_GOTO_OFF_F/S_GLBL_F).

examples/branches.sno walks all nine variants and prints which
branch fired; the expected output is in the file's trailing comment
block. Wired in as a demo and added to `just demos`.

Verified: just demos green (incl. new branches recipe), just test
green, single-direction :S / :F / :(L) / :(RETURN) / :(FRETURN)
unchanged, no fallthrough on the no-colon and reversed-order forms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git status

  This looks like the parser was extended to consume a leading :F correctly, but the underlying single-slot data structure (S_GTYP(S)
  per the lex source I cited in the brief) is still single-valued — so only the first parsed goto sticks.

message.content:
your description seems incorrect (L2 fired, I expected L1):
what does :S(L1):S(L2) do?  Or what is it for?

In standard SNOBOL4 semantics, this:

        expr :S(L1) :S(L2)

(or equivalently without spaces)

        expr :S(L1):S(L2)

is generally interpreted as multiple success transfers attached to the same statement.

But the key subtlety is:

transfers are processed left-to-right
the first taken transfer wins
transfering control exits the statement immediately

So:

        "ABC" "A" :S(L1):S(L2)

will go to L1, never L2.

Therefore :S(L2) is effectively dead/unreachable unless your implementation has unusual semantics.

Similarly:

        expr :F(L1):F(L2)

will always go to L1 on failure.

So why would anyone write this?

Usually one of:

1. Macro expansion artifact

A macro/preprocessor may append transfers mechanically.

Example:

# generated
PATTERN :S(TRACE)
PATTERN :S(USERLABEL)

becomes:

PATTERN :S(TRACE):S(USERLABEL)

where the generator did not realize the first transfer is terminal.

2. Programmer misunderstanding

Someone thought transfers were independent “handlers”:

:S(LOG):S(DONE)

expecting:

log
then done

But SNOBOL transfers are not callbacks; they are unconditional control transfers once triggered.

content.text: You're right — standard SNOBOL4 is left-to-right, first taken wins. My last-write-wins is wrong. Fixing this now as a follow-up: for both `:S(L1):S(L2)` and `:F(L1):F(L2)`, first wins; second is silently ignored (consistent with the standard).

input.new_string:
### Goto

Any statement may end with a goto suffix:

- `:(LBL)` -- unconditional jump
- `:S(LBL)` -- jump if the previous match (or test predicate)
  succeeded
- `:F(LBL)` -- jump if it failed
- `:(RETURN)` -- return from the current user-defined function
  (success return)
- `:(FRETURN)` -- return from the current user-defined function
  with a failed status

A statement may carry **both** an `:S` and an `:F` transfer. Every
combination of leading colons and ordering is accepted; the four
forms below are equivalent:

```
        STMT    :S(L1):F(L2)
        STMT    :S(L1) :F(L2)
        STMT    :S(L1)F(L2)        ; second goto without a colon prefix
        STMT    :F(L2):S(L1)        ; reversed order
```

`examples/branches.sno` exercises every form; run it with
`just branches`.

#### Goto precedence (left-to-right, first-wins)

SNOBOL4 transfers are processed left-to-right and a transfer that
fires exits the statement immediately, so any second transfer of the
**same direction** on one statement is unreachable. Duplicate-direction
gotos are silently dropped:

```
        EXPR    :S(L1):S(L2)        ; fires :S(L1); :S(L2) is dead code
        EXPR    :F(L1):F(L2)        ; fires :F(L1); :F(L2) is dead code
        EXPR    :S(L1):S(L2):F(L3)  ; fires :S(L1) on success or :F(L3)
                                    ; on failure; :S(L2) is dead code
```

This matches SPITBOL and the Bell Labs Macro Implementation. Such
forms typically appear as a macro-expansion artifact rather than as
intentional code; the compiler does not warn but the dead branch
will never run.

The `END` keyword on its own line marks the end of the program.

left-to-right and first-wins -- a transfer that fires exits the

duplicate; this commit makes us consistent with that.

second :S; when we already have an :F target (either as the primary

combined :S(L1):F(L2) and the reversed :F(L1):S(L2) keep working --
the first-wins rule applies per direction, not across directions.

content.content:
1	# Brief: SNOBOL4 silently drops gotos when statement has a nested function-call argument
2	
3	**Owner:** dcsno
4	**Branch:** `pr/nested-call-drops-gotos`
5	**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
6	**Discovered by:** dcftn during `milestone-1-fortran-compiler` saga (2026-05-08), in the wake of the `pr/combined-goto-parser` fix.
7	**Affects:** any SNOBOL4 statement of the shape
8	
9	```
10	        PRED(F(...), Y)    :S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
11	        PRED(X, F(...))    :S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
12	        PRED(F(...), G(..)):S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
13	```
14	
15	i.e. any predicate (IDENT, DIFFER, EQ, GT, etc.) whose argument list contains a nested function call (SUBSTR, SIZE, CHAR, etc.). All goto types -- `:S`, `:F`, and unconditional `:(LBL)` -- are silently dropped from such statements; the statement falls through regardless of the goto specified.
16	
17	This is a structural sibling of the combined-goto bug just fixed in `dcsno-combined-goto-parser.md`, but the manifestation is different and the repros need to be checked against this build.
18	
19	## Symptom
20	
21	When a SNOBOL4 statement evaluates a predicate (or function call) whose arguments include another function call, **the parser drops the goto on that statement**. The predicate evaluates and updates the success/failure flag correctly -- single-form gotos do still consult the flag in the dispatcher -- but no branch is ever taken because the goto target was never wired up.
22	
23	The bug is silent: no warning, no error, no diagnostic. The statement just falls through into the textually-next statement, producing programs that "almost work" but mis-route on every line where they were supposed to branch.
24	
25	## Repro (no-fallthrough regression)
26	
27	All four cases below run against the canonical `snobol4` wrapper on the deployed build (`snobol4.lgo` timestamp 2026-05-08 19:09:06).
28	
29	### Case 1: predicate that should SUCCEED, `:S` should fire
30	
31	```
32	$ cat /tmp/c1.sno
33	        IDENT(SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1), 'C')         :S(MATCH)
34	        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :S was DROPPED'   :(EX)
35	MATCH   OUTPUT = ':S fired (correct)'               :(EX)
36	EX      END
37	
38	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c1.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
39	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
40	fall through -- :S was DROPPED
41	```
42	
43	Expected `:S fired (correct)` because `SUBSTR('CAB',1,1) = 'C'` and `IDENT('C','C')` succeeds.
44	
45	### Case 2: predicate that should FAIL, `:F` should fire
46	
47	```
48	$ cat /tmp/c2.sno
49	        IDENT(SUBSTR('XYZ', 1, 1), 'C')         :F(FAIL)
50	        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :F was DROPPED'   :(EX)
51	FAIL    OUTPUT = ':F fired (correct)'               :(EX)
52	EX      END
53	
54	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c2.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
55	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
56	fall through -- :F was DROPPED
57	```
58	
59	Expected `:F fired (correct)` because `SUBSTR('XYZ',1,1) = 'X'` and `IDENT('X','C')` fails.
60	
61	### Case 3: unconditional `:(LBL)` -- also dropped
62	
63	```
64	$ cat /tmp/c3.sno
65	        IDENT(SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1), 'C')         :(JUMP)
66	        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :(LBL) was DROPPED' :(EX)
67	JUMP    OUTPUT = ':(LBL) fired (correct)'             :(EX)
68	EX      END
69	
70	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c3.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
71	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
72	fall through -- :(LBL) was DROPPED
73	```
74	
75	Expected `:(LBL) fired (correct)` because unconditional gotos always transfer.
76	
77	### Case 4: same-shape statement WITHOUT a nested call -- works correctly (control)
78	
79	```
80	$ cat /tmp/c4.sno
81	        A = SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1)
82	        IDENT(A, 'C')                           :S(MATCH)
83	        OUTPUT = 'fall through'                  :(EX)
84	MATCH   OUTPUT = ':S fired (correct)'            :(EX)
85	EX      END
86	
87	$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c4.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
88	          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
89	:S fired (correct)
90	```
91	
92	Identical predicate, same goto, but the SUBSTR result is extracted into a variable first. With no nested call in the statement's arg list, the goto is properly attached and fires.
93	
94	### Scope of the bug (smoke-tested against the same build)

file.content:
# Brief: SNOBOL4 silently drops gotos when statement has a nested function-call argument

**Owner:** dcsno
**Branch:** `pr/nested-call-drops-gotos`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
**Discovered by:** dcftn during `milestone-1-fortran-compiler` saga (2026-05-08), in the wake of the `pr/combined-goto-parser` fix.
**Affects:** any SNOBOL4 statement of the shape

```
        PRED(F(...), Y)    :S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
        PRED(X, F(...))    :S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
        PRED(F(...), G(..)):S(L) | :F(L) | :(L)
```

i.e. any predicate (IDENT, DIFFER, EQ, GT, etc.) whose argument list contains a nested function call (SUBSTR, SIZE, CHAR, etc.). All goto types -- `:S`, `:F`, and unconditional `:(LBL)` -- are silently dropped from such statements; the statement falls through regardless of the goto specified.

This is a structural sibling of the combined-goto bug just fixed in `dcsno-combined-goto-parser.md`, but the manifestation is different and the repros need to be checked against this build.

## Symptom

When a SNOBOL4 statement evaluates a predicate (or function call) whose arguments include another function call, **the parser drops the goto on that statement**. The predicate evaluates and updates the success/failure flag correctly -- single-form gotos do still consult the flag in the dispatcher -- but no branch is ever taken because the goto target was never wired up.

The bug is silent: no warning, no error, no diagnostic. The statement just falls through into the textually-next statement, producing programs that "almost work" but mis-route on every line where they were supposed to branch.

## Repro (no-fallthrough regression)

All four cases below run against the canonical `snobol4` wrapper on the deployed build (`snobol4.lgo` timestamp 2026-05-08 19:09:06).

### Case 1: predicate that should SUCCEED, `:S` should fire

```
$ cat /tmp/c1.sno
        IDENT(SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1), 'C')         :S(MATCH)
        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :S was DROPPED'   :(EX)
MATCH   OUTPUT = ':S fired (correct)'               :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c1.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
fall through -- :S was DROPPED
```

Expected `:S fired (correct)` because `SUBSTR('CAB',1,1) = 'C'` and `IDENT('C','C')` succeeds.

### Case 2: predicate that should FAIL, `:F` should fire

```
$ cat /tmp/c2.sno
        IDENT(SUBSTR('XYZ', 1, 1), 'C')         :F(FAIL)
        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :F was DROPPED'   :(EX)
FAIL    OUTPUT = ':F fired (correct)'               :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c2.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
fall through -- :F was DROPPED
```

Expected `:F fired (correct)` because `SUBSTR('XYZ',1,1) = 'X'` and `IDENT('X','C')` fails.

### Case 3: unconditional `:(LBL)` -- also dropped

```
$ cat /tmp/c3.sno
        IDENT(SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1), 'C')         :(JUMP)
        OUTPUT = 'fall through -- :(LBL) was DROPPED' :(EX)
JUMP    OUTPUT = ':(LBL) fired (correct)'             :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c3.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
fall through -- :(LBL) was DROPPED
```

Expected `:(LBL) fired (correct)` because unconditional gotos always transfer.

### Case 4: same-shape statement WITHOUT a nested call -- works correctly (control)

```
$ cat /tmp/c4.sno
        A = SUBSTR('CAB', 1, 1)
        IDENT(A, 'C')                           :S(MATCH)
        OUTPUT = 'fall through'                  :(EX)
MATCH   OUTPUT = ':S fired (correct)'            :(EX)
EX      END

$ snobol4 --load-binary /tmp/c4.sno@0x080000 --entry 0 \
          --quiet --speed 0 -n 10000000 -t 30
:S fired (correct)
```

Identical predicate, same goto, but the SUBSTR result is extracted into a variable first. With no nested call in the statement's arg list, the goto is properly attached and fires.

### Scope of the bug (smoke-tested against the same build)

| Statement | Goto | Expected | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IDENT(SUBSTR(s,p,l), Y)` | `:S(L)` | fire on `IDENT(F,Y)` success | dropped |
| `IDENT(X, SUBSTR(s,p,l))` | `:S(L)` | fire on success | dropped |
| `EQ(SIZE(s), n)`          | `:S(L)` | fire on success | dropped |
| `DIFFER(SUBSTR(s,p,l), Y)` | `:F(L)` | fire on failure | dropped |
| `IDENT(SUBSTR(s,p,l), Y)` | `:(L)` (unconditional) | always fire | dropped |
| `A = SUBSTR(s,p,l); IDENT(A, Y)` | `:S(L)` | fire on success | **fires (correct)** |

So the bug is gated on the presence of a nested function call in the statement's argument list. Extract the nested call to a local variable and the goto attaches normally.

## Hypothesised root cause

This looks like the inner function call's parsing or expression-stack handling is consuming the trailing colon and goto target tokens before the outer statement's TK_COLON handler runs. The lexer/parser may be over-greedy when parsing the inner call's argument list, walking past the closing `)` of the outer call and into the goto.

A second possibility: the codegen or AM lowering path for "predicate-with-nested-call" statements emits the predicate evaluation correctly but emits no branch dispatch. The success/failure flag is updated; nothing consults it because no branch op was emitted. (This would be analogous to the `S_GTYP(S)` single-slot bug fixed in `pr/combined-goto-parser` -- maybe nested-call statement types route through a code path that didn't get the same treatment.)

Worth grepping `src/sno_lex.plsw` and `src/sno_exec.plsw` for the statement-type routing of `ST_FN_CALL` (or whichever ST_* applies) and confirming the goto attachment / dispatch is wired up uniformly across statement types.

## Tests to add

1. **Case 1** above -- `:S` on nested-arg predicate, success path.
2. **Case 2** above -- `:F` on nested-arg predicate, failure path.
3. **Case 3** above -- `:(LBL)` on nested-arg statement.
4. **Combined `:S():F()` on nested-arg** -- compose with the just-shipped combined-goto fix.
5. **Pattern-match form with nested call** -- `STR pattern :S(L)` where `pattern` involves a function call, e.g. `'foo' BREAK(SUBSTR(',',1,1))`. Confirm gotos still attach.
6. **Control: variable subject** -- the extract-first form (Case 4) should remain green.

## Workaround (until the fix lands)

Extract every nested function-call result to a local variable first, then use the variable as the predicate argument. Verbose but works:

```
        X = SUBSTR(L, 1, 1)
        IDENT(X, 'C')                           :S(SKIP)
```

instead of

```
        IDENT(SUBSTR(L, 1, 1), 'C')             :S(SKIP)   ; goto dropped
```

dcftn's draft `snobol4/src/normalize.sno` was written in the inline-nested form throughout (col-1 char extraction, rstrip/lstrip loops, blank-line check, classify dispatch -- all use `IDENT(SUBSTR(...), ...)` or `EQ(SIZE(...), ...)`). The workaround would mean rewriting most of normalize.sno around explicit temp variables -- doable but defeats the dialect's natural idiom and is exactly the kind of friction that motivates the brief.

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No changes to single-form gotos with non-nested args -- they work.
- No changes to predicate evaluation (the success/failure flag is being computed correctly; just not consulted because the branch dispatch is missing).
- No changes to the combined-goto wiring just shipped in `pr/combined-goto-parser`.

## When done

Push `pr/nested-call-drops-gotos`. After mike relays + reinstalls the snobol4 binary:

- dcftn's `feat/m1-resume` saga can use the natural inline form `IDENT(SUBSTR(...), ...) :S(...)` throughout normalize / classify / expr / lower / emit_plsw, without preemptive extraction-to-local-variables.
- Any future SNOBOL4 program in any other repo using the documented nested-call form works as written.

## Why this surfaced now

The combined-goto fix (`pr/combined-goto-parser`, verified green at 19:09) re-enabled dcftn's testing pipeline for `normalize.sno`. With combined gotos working, the next layer of bug surfaced: even single gotos on nested-call statements are dropped. The combined-goto fix was necessary but not sufficient for the dialect to match its own documented surface.

# tools/briefs/

Saga briefs for the COR24 multi-agent ecosystem. Each brief is a self-contained spec for a saga: the agent reads it, develops on `feat/<slug>`, renames to `pr/<slug>` when ready, signals mike, mike relays.

## How briefs work

- **Filename convention:** `<target>-<saga-slug>.md`. `<target>` is either a single agent (e.g. `dcxas-cor24-asm-cli.md`) or a generic prefix (`dc-`, `dw-`) for multi-agent briefs.
- **Branch convention — feat→pr rename:**
  - **`feat/<slug>`** = work-in-progress. Agents create this with `dg-new-feature <slug>` (which cuts from `origin/dev`).
  - **`pr/<slug>`** = signal that the saga is **ready for relay**. Created by renaming `feat/<slug>` → `pr/<slug>` via `dg-mark-pr` once the work is complete and tested.
  - The branch shape **is** the readiness signal. Never start a saga on `pr/<slug>` directly — `dg-list-pr` would see it as ready and `dg-relay` could integrate WIP.
- **Workflow:** agent reads brief → `dg-new-feature <slug>` (creates `feat/<slug>` from `dev`) → implements + tests → `dg-mark-pr` (renames to `pr/<slug>`) → signals mike → mike `dg-relay`s → mike promotes `dev → main` when ready (separate, on-demand step).
- **Agents may draft cross-repo briefs.** If an agent diagnoses a blocker in another repo (e.g. a tc24r limitation), they can draft a brief for the responsible agent and drop it directly here. Mike reviews at relay time. See `feedback_agent_drafted_briefs.md` in the project memory.
- **Permissions:** dir is `drwxrwsr-x mike:devgroup`. Mike-authored briefs have mode `640 mike:devgroup`. Agent-drafted briefs inherit `<agent>:devgroup` ownership.

## 🏛️ Architecture: compilers, wrappers, demos

Each language repo (`sw-cor24-<lang>`) builds **a compiler/interpreter** for that language on COR24. That compiler is the repo's main artifact. Demos under `examples/` exercise the compiler.

Wrappers on PATH (`work/bin/<lang>`) invoke the compiler. **Two valid packagings for the shipped compiler** — mike picks at install time:

- **Bundled `.lgo`** (e.g. `plsw.lgo`): single self-contained image. Wrapper is a thin pass-through: `exec cor24-emu --lgo $TOOLROOT/../lib/cor24/<lang>.lgo "$@"`.
- **Script-composed**: wrapper is a shell script that runs `cor24-emu --lgo <interpreter>.lgo --load-binary <compiler>.sno@<addr> ...`. Useful when the compiler is itself a program in another language that runs inside an interpreter image (e.g. Fortran-in-SNOBOL4 — `fortran` could compose `snobol4.lgo` + `fortran-compiler.sno` at runtime instead of pre-bundling).

Both packagings are equivalent for users; the choice is about build-time bundling. Future briefs/sagas don't constrain agents to one or the other.

Demos and demo outputs (e.g. `examples/hello.f`, `examples/hello.lgo`) live in the repo's own `examples/` directory and are **not** installed to `work/lib/cor24/` — only compilers/interpreters live there.

| 4 | `dwftn-hello-world-demo.md` | 🔵 in flight (rework after first attempt went out of scope) |

The first three landed and verified end-to-end. dwftn's web demo is the only remaining piece for the Fortran live demo to ship.

* branches.sno -- demonstrates correct behaviour of every SNOBOL4
* conditional-transfer (goto) form. Companion regression for the
* combined :S(...) :F(...) parser fix (dcsno-combined-goto-parser).
*
* Each test prints which branch fired so a reader can eyeball the
* output. The expected output is at the bottom.

* --- 1. :S(L) on a predicate that SUCCEEDS -> S fires ----------
        OUTPUT = '1: :S(L) succ'
        IDENT('A', 'A')                          :S(T1OK)
        OUTPUT = '   1 fall-through (BUG: :S did not fire)'  :(T2)
T1OK    OUTPUT = '   1 :S fired'                 :(T2)

* --- 2. :S(L) on a predicate that FAILS -> fall through -------
T2      OUTPUT = '2: :S(L) fail -> fallthrough'
        IDENT('A', 'B')                          :S(T2BAD)
        OUTPUT = '   2 fall-through (correct)'   :(T3)
T2BAD   OUTPUT = '   2 :S fired (BUG)'           :(T3)

* --- 3. :F(L) on a predicate that FAILS -> F fires -----------
T3      OUTPUT = '3: :F(L) fail'
        IDENT('A', 'B')                          :F(T3OK)
        OUTPUT = '   3 fall-through (BUG: :F did not fire)'  :(T4)
T3OK    OUTPUT = '   3 :F fired'                 :(T4)

* --- 4. Combined :S(L1):F(L2) -- predicate FAILS -> F branch fires --
T4      OUTPUT = '4: :S(L):F(L) fail -> F'
        IDENT('A', 'B')                          :S(T4S):F(T4F)
        OUTPUT = '   4 fall-through (BUG: F branch dropped)'  :(T5)
T4S     OUTPUT = '   4 :S fired (BUG: predicate failed)' :(T5)
T4F     OUTPUT = '   4 :F fired'                 :(T5)

* --- 5. Combined :S(L1):F(L2) -- predicate SUCCEEDS -> S branch fires --
T5      OUTPUT = '5: :S(L):F(L) succ -> S'
        IDENT('A', 'A')                          :S(T5S):F(T5F)

T5S     OUTPUT = '   5 :S fired'                 :(T6)
T5F     OUTPUT = '   5 :F fired (BUG)'            :(T6)

* --- 6. No-colon-on-second-goto :S(L1)F(L2) -- predicate fails -> F --

T7S     OUTPUT = '   7 :S fired'                 :(T8)

* --- 8. Reverse order :F(L1):S(L2) -- predicate fails -> F ---
T8      OUTPUT = '8: :F(L):S(L) fail -> F'

        OUTPUT = '   8 fall-through (BUG)'        :(T9)
T8S     OUTPUT = '   8 :S fired (BUG)'            :(T9)
T8F     OUTPUT = '   8 :F fired'                 :(T9)

* --- 9. Unconditional goto :(L) ------------------------------
T9      OUTPUT = '9: :(L) unconditional'
                                                 :(T9JUMP)

T9JUMP  OUTPUT = '   9 :(L) fired'               :(T10)

* --- 10. Pathological :S(L1):S(L2) -- left-to-right, first wins ---

git add docs/language-reference.md examples/branches.sno src/sno_exec.plsw src/sno_lex.plsw && git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix: nested SUBSTR/SIZE/CHAR in builtin predicate args

Statements like  IDENT(SUBSTR('CAB',1,1), 'C')  silently dropped
their goto because the lexer's builtin-predicate arg parser only
recognised simple IDENT/INT/STR primitives. Hitting the inner `(`
of SUBSTR mid-arg, the parser stored "SUBSTR" as a plain OE_IDENT
(referring to a non-existent variable) and then walked off the end
of arg2 with TT stuck on the inner `(`. The trailing
`:S(L)` / `:F(L)` / `:(L)` got swallowed by the EOL-skip loop.

Fix:

* sno_lex.plsw -- new PARSE_NESTED_FN PROC that handles SUBSTR(s,p,l),
  SIZE(s), and CHAR(c) inline. Returns the new EPI on success or the
  starting EPI on no-match. Wired into both arg1 and arg2 positions
  of the builtin-predicate parser; falls back to the existing simple
  IDENT/INT/STR path when the IDENT isn't a known nested function.
  Slot layout matches the assignment-context parser: each arg pushes
  one or more EP slots ending with a function-marker (OE_SUBSTR /
  OE_SIZE / OE_CHAR).

* sno_exec.plsw -- the S_TYP=4 (builtin predicate) lowering now walks
  all S_EPCNT slots (not just two) and dispatches on EP_TYP, emitting
  OP_SUBSTR / OP_SIZE / OP_CHAR for the call markers. The slot stream
  is postfix: each primitive pushes a value, each marker pops its
  args and pushes its result. After the loop the predicate has
  exactly two values on the stack regardless of nesting depth.

examples/branches.sno extends to 17 cases (added 13-17 covering the
arg1-nested, arg2-nested, EQ(SIZE(...),...), and unconditional-goto
forms). docs/language-reference.md notes the supported nested
functions in the goto section. just demos / just test green.

1	# Brief: design SNOBOL4's storage runtime over PL/SW primitives
2	
3	**Owner:** dcsno
4	**Branch:** `pr/storage-allocation-runtime`
5	**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
6	**Prerequisite:** read
7	`/disk1/.../work/dcpls/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-plsw/docs/storage-allocation.md`
8	first. That doc describes the PL/SW substrate this saga builds
9	on. As of dcpls's `pr/storage-macros` + `pr/getmain-freemain-macros`,
10	the substrate is **fully shipped**: `include/_plsw_storage.msw`
11	provides `_PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE)` and `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(USERADDR, LEN)`
12	procedures over a free-list-backed heap (default 64 KB,
13	configurable via `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE`), AND PL/I-flavored
14	`?GETMAIN(LENGTH, ADDRESS, RC)` / `?FREEMAIN(LENGTH, ADDRESS, RC)`
15	macros wrapping them. Reg-rs cases `plsw_storage_*` cover alloc,
16	coalesce, OOM, double-free, and size-mismatch using the macro form.
17	
18	You can implement against either surface today.
19	
20	## Context
21	
22	SNOBOL4 on PL/SW has a high-frequency allocation pattern:
23	parsing source, building pattern objects, evaluating matches,
24	backtracking, building strings. Today the SNOBOL4 source under
25	`sw-cor24-snobol4/src/` either doesn't allocate (uses static
26	buffers) or rolls a bump arena ad hoc. As `compiler.sno` and
27	larger programs land, this stops scaling.
28	
29	The PL/SW design doc lays out a clean layering:
30	
31	> PL/SW provides only the raw alloc/free primitives. Region
32	> boundaries, mark/reclaim, and garbage collection live in the
33	> consumer's runtime.
34	
35	That means `include/_plsw_storage.msw` gives SNOBOL4 the
36	`?GETMAIN SET(P) LENGTH(N) RC(rc);` /
37	`?FREEMAIN ADDR(P) LENGTH(N) RC(rc);` macros (which expand to
38	`P = _PLSW_GETMAIN(N); ...` and `rc = _PLSW_FREEMAIN(P, N);`
39	respectively) plus the underlying procedures
40	`_PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE)` and `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(ADDR, LEN)`. RC values:
41	GETMAIN 0=success / 4=OOM; FREEMAIN 0=success / 1=double-free /
42	2=size-mismatch. **Anything beyond those primitives — region
43	save/restore, mark/sweep, generational GC, per-context heaps —
44	is yours.**
45	
46	Why this split: Prolog wants WAM-style trail unwinding, future
47	Fortran wants common-block static + stack frames, future C-like
48	guests want plain malloc/free. Each has its own storage policy
49	on top of the same dumb substrate. SNOBOL4's policy lives in
50	SNOBOL4's runtime.
51	
52	## Goal
53	
54	After this saga: SNOBOL4 has a documented, implemented storage
55	runtime that scales to the workloads it'll see (`compiler.sno`,
56	pattern-heavy demos, etc.). The runtime calls `?GETMAIN` /
57	`?FREEMAIN` (or the underlying `_PLSW_GETMAIN`/`_PLSW_FREEMAIN`
58	procedures) as primitives and adds whatever policy SNOBOL4
59	needs on top.
60	
61	## Two reasonable designs to choose from
62	
63	Both are valid. Pick the one that fits SNOBOL4's actual
64	allocation profile; this brief is not prescriptive about which.
65	
66	### Design A: GC over a single big region
67	
68	- One `?GETMAIN SET(BASE) LENGTH(BIG) RC(RET);` at startup carves
69	  out the whole SNOBOL4 heap (e.g. 32 KB or 64 KB).
70	- SNOBOL4's runtime owns that region: cell allocator, mark/sweep
71	  (or copying) GC, root-set traversal of the SNOBOL4 stack /
72	  variable table, etc. PL/SW's free-list is never touched after
73	  startup; `?FREEMAIN` is called once at program exit (or never).
74	- Pros: traditional SNOBOL4 model, no per-cell PL/SW call
75	  overhead, full control over headers and tags, handles arbitrary
76	  liveness graphs.
77	- Cons: more code (a real GC). Need a precise root set, which
78	  means cooperating with PL/SW's calling convention to find live
79	  cells in stack frames and registers.
80	
81	### Design B: region-stack over `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN`
82	
83	- Multiple `?GETMAIN SET(REGION) LENGTH(REGION_SIZE) RC(RET);`
84	  blocks form a stack of regions (think arena-per-pattern-match-attempt).
85	- Each match attempt pushes a region; on backtrack, the region
86	  is `?FREEMAIN`'d wholesale.
87	- Long-lived data (symbol table, compiled patterns) lives in a
88	  base region that's never popped.
89	- Pros: simpler than full GC; matches SNOBOL4's natural
90	  pattern-match scope structure; fragmentation is bounded
91	  because each region is freed wholesale.
92	- Cons: cells that escape a region (e.g. captured by an outer
93	  match) need explicit promotion to an older region or
94	  copy-out. Cells that don't escape are free; cells that do
95	  cost the copy.
96	
97	A third hybrid (small fixed-size cell pool for high-churn
98	allocations, region-stack for variable-size work, GC only over
99	the symbol table) is also possible. Whichever approach you take,
100	**the doc-of-record for "what is SNOBOL4's storage model" lives
101	in `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/`**, not in PL/SW.
102	
103	## What this saga delivers
104	
105	Pick one of these scopes; both are reasonable as standalone
106	sagas:
107	
108	- **Scope A: Design + plan only.** Audit current allocation
109	  sites, write `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/storage.md` describing
110	  the chosen runtime model (A, B, or hybrid), draft an interface
111	  for the runtime procedures (e.g. `_SNO_ALLOC_CELL`,
112	  `_SNO_GC_COLLECT`), but don't implement yet. Implementation is
113	  a follow-up saga.
114	- **Scope B: Design + minimum runtime.** Same docs as Scope A
115	  plus an MVP of the chosen runtime — enough to handle
116	  `examples/hello.sno` and one pattern-matching demo without
117	  static buffers. Subsequent sagas widen coverage.
118	
119	Pick whichever fits your bandwidth. If unsure, do Scope A first
120	— design errors here are cheap to fix on paper, expensive to fix
121	in shipped runtime code.
122	
123	## Migration mapping (when ready)
124	
125	For Scope B (or for whenever the runtime lands), each existing
126	allocation site moves from `DCL ... BYTE; DCL ... INT INIT(0);`
127	ad-hoc bump arenas to either:
128	
129	```pl/i
130	?GETMAIN  SET(P)  LENGTH(N) RC(RET);
131	/* ... use P ... */
132	?FREEMAIN ADDR(P) LENGTH(N) RC(RET);
133	```
134	
135	… or a SNOBOL4-runtime call that wraps `?GETMAIN` with policy:
136	
137	```pl/i
138	P = SNO_ALLOC_CELL(KIND_STRING, length);
139	/* ... use P ... */
140	/* GC reclaims when no longer reachable */
141	```
142	
143	Inventory your existing call sites with:
144	```sh
145	grep -nE 'ARENA_POS|arena_alloc|ALLOC.*PROC' sw-cor24-snobol4/src/
146	```
147	
148	## What goes in this PR (Scope A version)
149	
150	1. Audit of existing allocation sites in `src/`.
151	2. `docs/storage.md` describing the chosen runtime model.
152	3. Drafted interface for `_SNO_ALLOC_*` (or whatever names fit)
153	   procedures.
154	4. Plan for which allocation sites move first when the runtime
155	   ships.
156	5. Optional: a sample `.plsw` showing the call shape, against a
157	   stub `_PLSW_GETMAIN` that returns 0 (so the design is at
158	   least syntactically validated against PL/SW today).
159	
160	## What does NOT go in this PR
161	
162	- No `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` source — that's dcpls's saga
163	  (`pr/storage-macros`). Don't implement the substrate; depend
164	  on it.
165	- No PL/SW compiler or macro changes.
166	- No SNOBOL4 language changes (no `.sno` source rewrites).
167	- No allocation runtime that conflicts with the eventual
168	  PL/SW substrate (e.g. don't reimplement `?GETMAIN`'s job in
169	  SNOBOL4 source — call it).
170	
171	## When done
172	
173	Push `pr/storage-allocation-runtime` and signal mike. Promotion
174	to `dev`/`main` is mike's call. After dcpls's `pr/storage-macros`
175	ships, SNOBOL4's runtime can land in a follow-up saga (or this
176	saga's Scope B can be extended in place if not yet relayed).
177	
178	## Questions to answer in your design doc
179	
180	1. What is the dominant allocation size in SNOBOL4? (Tiny cells?
181	   Medium strings? Variable patterns?) The answer should drive
182	   the choice between Design A (GC over big region) and Design B
183	   (region-stack).
184	2. What is the rooted set during pattern matching? (i.e. which
185	   pointers must remain valid across a `?GETMAIN`?) If you can't
186	   enumerate this concisely, GC is harder; region-stack may be a
187	   better fit.
188	3. Are there any natural "scope boundaries" in SNOBOL4 execution
189	   where you could drop everything cheaply? (Match attempt?
190	   Statement boundary? Function call?) Region-stack maps cleanly
191	   onto these.
192	4. Worst-case live set — how big can the SNOBOL4 heap get before
193	   you'd consider it pathological? That sets the reasonable
194	   default for `PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` in your `%INCLUDE plsw_storage`
195	   line.

## What goes in this PR (Scope A version)

1. Audit of existing allocation sites in `src/`.
2. `docs/storage.md` describing the chosen runtime model.
3. Drafted interface for `_SNO_ALLOC_*` (or whatever names fit)
   procedures.
4. Plan for which allocation sites move first when the runtime
   ships.
5. Optional: a sample `.plsw` showing the call shape, against a

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` source — that's dcpls's saga
  (`pr/storage-macros`). Don't implement the substrate; depend

- No PL/SW compiler or macro changes.
- No SNOBOL4 language changes (no `.sno` source rewrites).
- No allocation runtime that conflicts with the eventual

saga's Scope B can be extended in place if not yet relayed).

## Questions to answer in your design doc

1. What is the dominant allocation size in SNOBOL4? (Tiny cells?
   Medium strings? Variable patterns?) The answer should drive
   the choice between Design A (GC over big region) and Design B
   (region-stack).
2. What is the rooted set during pattern matching? (i.e. which
   pointers must remain valid across a `?GETMAIN`?) If you can't
   enumerate this concisely, GC is harder; region-stack may be a
   better fit.
3. Are there any natural "scope boundaries" in SNOBOL4 execution

   Statement boundary? Function call?) Region-stack maps cleanly
   onto these.
4. Worst-case live set — how big can the SNOBOL4 heap get before
   you'd consider it pathological? That sets the reasonable
   default for `PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` in your `%INCLUDE plsw_storage`

1	# SNOBOL4 language reference
2	
3	This is the language as actually implemented by the interpreter in
4	this repository, not the full historical SNOBOL4. It documents which
5	statement forms, builtins, pattern primitives, and limits the
6	interpreter currently supports. Use it as a cheat sheet when writing
7	or porting `.sno` programs.
8	
9	The interpreter is built from four PL/SW modules:
10	
11	- `src/sno_main.plsw` -- driver: `MAIN`, calls `READ_SRC` /
12	  `PARSE` / `LOWER_ALL` / `AM_EXEC`.
13	- `src/sno_util.plsw` -- I/O helpers: `READ_SRC`, `READ_INPUT`.
14	- `src/sno_lex.plsw` -- lexer + parser + AM emit.
15	- `src/sno_exec.plsw` -- lowering + executor + pattern matching +
16	  builtins.
17	
18	Plus opcode definitions in `include/am.msw`, shared globals and
19	limits in `include/snoglob.msw`, and runtime headers in
20	`include/{descr,heap,pat}.msw`. Built by `scripts/build-modular.sh`
21	into `build/snobol4.bin`. When you suspect something isn't supported,
22	grep `src/sno_*.plsw` and `include/*.msw` first.
23	
24	## Lexical rules
25	
26	- Source is loaded into a fixed buffer (8 KB cap, see SRC limit
27	  below). Each line is one statement; comments are lines whose first
28	  non-blank character is `*`.
29	- A line that starts in column 1 with an identifier defines a label
30	  whose name is that identifier. Statements not at column 1 have no
31	  label.
32	- String literals use single or double quotes (`'...'` or `"..."`).
33	  No escape sequences. Max literal length is 127 characters.
34	- Identifiers are uppercase letters and digits, max 7 effective
35	  characters (longer identifiers are accepted by the lexer but
36	  truncated to 7 in the symbol-table slot, so they will collide).
37	- Lowercase letters in identifiers are folded to uppercase.
38	- `INPUT` reads a line from a data file (batch mode) or live UART
39	  (interactive mode). Either way, the read line is **uppercased
40	  in place** before being returned -- this is by design so that
41	  pattern matching with literal keywords stays case-insensitive.
42	
43	## Statements
44	
45	### Assignment
46	
47	```
48	        VAR = expr
49	LBL     VAR = expr
50	```
51	
52	`expr` may be:
53	
54	- A string literal: `'hello'`
55	- An integer literal: `42`
56	- A variable reference: `S`
57	- A binary expression: `A + B`, `A - B`, `A * B` (also unary minus
58	  via `0 - X`)
59	- `REMDR(A, B)` -- integer modulo (the only multi-arg arithmetic
60	  builtin)
61	- `INPUT` -- reads one line; fails (`:F`) at end of input
62	- A concatenation: `'P: ' S` -- juxtaposed parts (max 8 parts per
63	  statement, same `EPSLOTS` budget as pattern parts). Concat operands
64	  may mix strings and ints; ints are rendered as decimal.
65	- `ARRAY('1:N')` -- allocate an array with integer indices 1..N
66	- An array element: `NAMES<I>` or `NAMES<3>`
67	- A user function call: `FOO(X)` (after `DEFINE('FOO(X)')`)
68	
69	### Pattern match
70	
71	```
72	        SUBJ pattern... :S(YES) :F(NO)
73	LBL     SUBJ pattern... :S(YES) :F(NO)
74	```
75	
76	A statement whose first token after the (optional) label is a
77	variable, immediately followed by another token (not `=`), is a
78	pattern match. The pattern is built from the parts listed in
79	[Pattern parts](#pattern-parts) below. Up to 8 parts per statement.
80	
81	There is **no pattern-replacement assignment**. Standard SNOBOL4
82	allows `S pattern = replacement` to mutate the subject in place;
83	this interpreter only matches, never replaces. To rewrite a string
84	you must build a new one.
85	
86	### Goto
87	
88	Any statement may end with a goto suffix:
89	
90	- `:(LBL)` -- unconditional jump
91	- `:S(LBL)` -- jump if the previous match (or test predicate)
92	  succeeded
93	- `:F(LBL)` -- jump if it failed
94	- `:(RETURN)` -- return from the current user-defined function
95	  (success return)
96	- `:(FRETURN)` -- return from the current user-defined function
97	  with a failed status
98	
99	A statement may carry **both** an `:S` and an `:F` transfer. Every
100	combination of leading colons and ordering is accepted; the four
101	forms below are equivalent:
102	
103	```
104	        STMT    :S(L1):F(L2)
105	        STMT    :S(L1) :F(L2)
106	        STMT    :S(L1)F(L2)        ; second goto without a colon prefix
107	        STMT    :F(L2):S(L1)        ; reversed order
108	```
109	
110	`examples/branches.sno` exercises every form; run it with
111	`just branches`.
112	
113	#### Goto precedence (left-to-right, first-wins)
114	
115	SNOBOL4 transfers are processed left-to-right and a transfer that
116	fires exits the statement immediately, so any second transfer of the
117	**same direction** on one statement is unreachable. Duplicate-direction
118	gotos are silently dropped:
119	
120	```
121	        EXPR    :S(L1):S(L2)        ; fires :S(L1); :S(L2) is dead code
122	        EXPR    :F(L1):F(L2)        ; fires :F(L1); :F(L2) is dead code
123	        EXPR    :S(L1):S(L2):F(L3)  ; fires :S(L1) on success or :F(L3)
124	                                    ; on failure; :S(L2) is dead code
125	```
126	
127	This matches SPITBOL and the Bell Labs Macro Implementation. Such
128	forms typically appear as a macro-expansion artifact rather than as
129	intentional code; the compiler does not warn but the dead branch
130	will never run.
131	
132	The `END` keyword on its own line marks the end of the program.
133	
134	### REFLECT
135	
136	```
137	        REFLECT VAR
138	LBL     REFLECT VAR
139	```
140	
141	In-place pronoun swap on a string variable. See
142	[REFLECT](#reflect-pronoun-swap) below for the table of swaps.
143	
144	### DUMP
145	
146	```
147	        DUMP
148	```
149	
150	Print the current values of all integer variables (debug aid).
151	
152	## Pattern parts
153	
154	| part            | meaning                                                |
155	|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
156	| `'literal'`     | match an exact substring                               |
157	| `SPAN(class)`   | consume a maximal run of chars drawn from `class`      |
158	| `BREAK(class)`  | consume up to (not including) any char in `class`      |
159	| `LEN(N)`        | consume exactly N chars (`N` may be int or variable)  |
160	| `REM`           | consume the rest of the subject                        |
161	| `var`           | match the run-time value of `var` as a literal         |
162	| `. VAR`         | capture the most recently matched span into `VAR`      |
163	
164	`class` is a string literal whose characters form the alphabet for
165	that part. Pattern matching is unanchored: the engine tries each
166	starting position in the subject until one of them matches the
167	whole pattern, or every position has been tried (then it fails).
168	
169	There is no `LEN(0)` issue; matching zero chars succeeds at the
170	current cursor.
171	
172	Patterns currently **not** supported (would require interpreter
173	extension):
174	
175	- `ANY(class)` (single char from a class)
176	- `NOTANY(class)`
177	- Pattern alternation `|`
178	- Conditional / immediate value assignment `$ VAR`
179	- Recursion via `*PATTERN`
180	- The `ARB`, `BAL`, `POS`, `RPOS`, `TAB`, `RTAB`, `SUCCEED`, `FAIL`
181	  primitives
182	
183	## Builtins (predicate-style)
184	
185	These return success or failure for `:S` / `:F` branching. They
186	are 2-arg only.
187	
188	| builtin       | meaning                                |
189	|---------------|----------------------------------------|
190	| `IDENT(A,B)`  | succeeds if A and B are identical      |
191	| `DIFFER(A,B)` | succeeds if A and B differ             |
192	| `GT(A,B)`     | A > B                                  |
193	| `EQ(A,B)`     | A = B                                  |
194	| `LE(A,B)`     | A <= B                                 |
195	
196	There is no `LT`, `GE`, or `NE`. Use `:F` on `LE`/`GT`/etc. to get
197	the opposite.
198	
199	## Builtins (value-returning)
200	
201	| builtin              | meaning                                  |
202	|----------------------|------------------------------------------|
203	| `REMDR(A,B)`         | integer A mod B                          |
